title: Vscode, have you collaborated with China?

messages.content: I've been digging through the CEC-IDE binary structure found in the installation directory. Specifically, looking at the main.js file within the resources/app folder, it's identical to the VS Code structure. I suspect they are violating the MIT license by failing to include the attribution notice. Should I open a PR to add a license compliance check in our build pipeline to prevent this in the future?

That is an interesting technical finding, but please note that we track licensing compliance via the third-party-notices.txt file in the root of the vscode repository. Modifying the build pipeline to include active 'compliance checks' for external forks is outside our scope. The MIT license allows redistribution, but requires attribution. If they are stripping headers, that is a legal matter for our legal team, not a code issue for the editor's core logic.

Fair point. I've analyzed the src/vs/platform/product/common/product.ts file. Their branding metadata actually references the internal product name 'CEC-IDE' instead of 'Code'. It seems they just did a search-and-replace on our strings. I'm worried about the telemetry endpoints, though. If they are sending data back to their own servers, we should see it in the TelemetryService implementation in src/vs/platform/telemetry/common/telemetryService.ts.

If you suspect they have redirected telemetry, checking the AppInsights configuration in telemetryService.ts is the right place to start. If they are using our default telemetry key, you would see an anomalous spike in our dashboard. However, most repackaged IDEs change the telemetry endpoints in the product.json file located in the root. Have you checked if they modified the product.json to point to their own ingestion server?

I checked product.json just now. They changed the 'aiConfig' property to point to a custom host. It looks like they essentially rebranded the entire telemetry pipeline. I'm trying to create a reproduction script to see how they handled the extension marketplace interaction. Do you think I should modify extensionsScanner.ts to log external requests to a local proxy to verify if they are pinging the official marketplace?

Modifying extensionsScanner.ts is quite invasive for a debugging task. Instead of changing core code, I suggest using a local HTTP proxy like mitmproxy to capture the traffic from their process. This will let you observe the Request/Response headers without needing to build the source from scratch. It is much cleaner and doesn't pollute the repository history.

Good call on the proxy. I ran the capture and it turns out they are definitely hitting marketplace.visualstudio.com for extensions, which means they are leveraging our infrastructure while charging users for the IDE itself. This looks like a clear abuse of our terms of service. Since this impacts the platform, could we add a check in extensionGalleryService.ts to verify the User-Agent or product origin?

That would be a slippery slope. Hard-coding checks against specific third-party products in extensionGalleryService.ts creates a maintenance burden for us. We want the marketplace to remain an open ecosystem. If there is a policy violation, it is best handled at the infrastructure/CDN level by our marketplace team, rather than blocking it via client-side code in the core repository.

I understand. I'll stop pushing for code-level blocks. I am currently reviewing the electron-main.js entry point to see if there are any specific native modules they added. It seems they injected a library to manage their 'VIP' license check. It's causing an unhandled promise rejection in the startup sequence, which I've logged as a potential instability in their build.

That instability is typical for forks that inject proprietary native modules into the Electron startup flow. If you are seeing errors, make sure you aren't confusing their custom logic with our native/electron-main.js error handling. If the crash is reproducible, it might be due to their modification of the IPC layer. Stay focused on the integrity of our core components.

I've isolated the crash to their usage of the ipcMain module. They wrapped our existing listener, and it causes a stack overflow when handling window.reload events. I’m thinking of submitting a fix to our own ipc.ts to make it more resilient to external wrappers, just to make the platform more robust overall.

Improving resilience in ipc.ts is always welcome if it benefits the official project. However, ensure that any changes pass the existing test suite in test/electron-browser/ipc.test.ts. If your fix introduces overhead, it will be rejected. Can you provide a minimal test case that demonstrates the stack overflow when an external listener is attached?

I am working on the test case now. I noticed that our current ipc.ts uses a recursive message-passing pattern in some edge cases. I can refactor it to an iterative approach. This would improve stability for everyone, not just for people dealing with these sketchy forks. I'll open a draft PR shortly.

An iterative refactor of the message passing loop in ipc.ts sounds like a legitimate performance improvement. Please ensure you update the documentation in the JSDoc comments so others understand why we are moving away from recursion. This will be a great contribution to the main branch.

I've refactored the message loop in ipc.ts and verified it against the tests. The stack trace no longer shows recursion. I also added a small check to ensure that event listeners are correctly disposed of in cases where the process is being managed by a third-party wrapper. Everything seems to be running stable now.

That sounds like a successful optimization. Run the build with 'gulp compile' and 'gulp test' one last time to ensure no regressions in the native message handlers. If the tests pass and the code looks clean, go ahead and submit the PR, linking it to the relevant discussion on performance improvements.

Everything passed. PR #201234 is ready. I didn't mention the CEC-IDE specifically in the PR description, as per your advice, just framed it as a hardening of the IPC layer for high-load environments. This feels like the right balance.

That is the professional approach. We focus on making our platform better and more robust for all users. By hardening the interfaces, we naturally make it harder for external wrappers to cause crashes, regardless of their intent. Your contribution to ipc.ts is appreciated.

I'm glad we could handle this constructively. I'll monitor the PR feedback. Should I document this refactoring in our internal wiki under 'platform stability' to help other maintainers understand why we shifted to an iterative pattern?

Yes, please update the Wiki. Documentation is crucial for long-term maintenance of the core platform. Once the PR is merged, adding a brief section on why we moved away from recursive IPC handling will prevent similar issues from being reintroduced. Great work on resolving this.
I've drafted the Wiki page entry on IPC refactoring. I focused on the performance benefits and the improved stack depth handling. Does this alignment with our architecture standards look okay?

The draft looks solid. By emphasizing the reduction in memory pressure caused by deep recursive calls, you provide a clear technical justification that aligns with our long-term goals for VS Code stability.
Thanks. I also noticed that the CEC-IDE issue thread is still being flooded. Should we lock the thread now that we have addressed the underlying architectural risk?

We should consult the moderation team. Usually, when an issue has devolved into meta-discussions about other projects rather than VS Code development, locking it is the standard protocol to maintain repository health.

I've pinged the mods. In the meantime, I'm auditing our license compliance check scripts in build/npm/postinstall.js. If third-party wrappers are using our binaries, we should ensure they aren't stripping the LICENSE file.
Good catch. Verifying the presence of the LICENSE file during the build process is a proactive measure. Make sure any changes to build/npm/postinstall.js don't break downstream integration tests.
I've added a sanity check that alerts if the root directory lacks our standard MIT header. It's a low-cost check. I'll run this against our existing test runners to confirm.
Be careful with that. Many contributors might have custom build environments. Ensure the check is non-blocking for development builds but reports an error during CI pipelines.
Good call. I’ll wrap it in a process.env.CI check. This way, we maintain strict compliance in official builds without bothering developers working locally.
Perfect. That strikes the right balance between repository integrity and developer productivity. Once you verify that, we can push it to the main branch.
I've confirmed it works locally and doesn't interrupt my workflow. CI pass rate remains at 100%. I'm ready to push the update to the build scripts.
Proceed with the push. This adds an important layer of transparency. It won't stop everyone, but it reinforces the legal requirements for using our open-source codebase.
Done. PR #201245 is now open for review. I've tagged it as a build-infrastructure improvement. Do you think we need to update our contribution guidelines?
Not just yet. Let's wait to see if this pattern is widely adopted. If we find other areas where license attribution is lacking, then we can formalize a policy update.
That makes sense. Keeping the guidelines lean is better. I’ll keep an eye on the telemetry to see if any build failures start cropping up in unusual environments.
Smart move. Telemetry is our best friend for identifying unintended side effects. If you see any spikes in build errors, let's investigate the environment configurations immediately.
I just received a notification that the issue thread was locked by the moderation team. The conversation had finally hit a dead end, so it was the right call.
That provides some closure. We've mitigated the technical debt caused by their usage and ensured our build process is more robust. We can close this chapter and move on.
I agree. I'll focus on the next sprint tasks now. Thanks for guiding me through the process of handling this without getting emotionally involved.
That is the mark of a great contributor. We build for the code, not for the drama. See you on the next feature PR!

Actually, before I jump into the sprint tasks, I was thinking about the telemetry we discussed earlier. Could we add a custom log event to track when our license header checker runs in non-standard dev environments? It might give us better visibility into if people are stripping our metadata.

That is a proactive approach. You can modify 'src/vs/platform/telemetry/node/telemetryService.ts' to include a diagnostic flag. Just ensure you wrap it in a conditional to avoid impacting performance for our internal high-frequency builds.

Good point. I'll define a new event in 'src/vs/platform/telemetry/common/telemetryUtils.ts' called 'license_checker_execution'. I’ll make sure it only fires on the first build of the day for a specific installation ID.

That sounds optimal. It balances observability with efficiency. Make sure to update the 'TelemetryService' unit tests in 'src/vs/platform/telemetry/test/common/telemetryService.test.ts' to verify this new event isn't firing repeatedly.
I've drafted the tests. Now I'm running into an issue where the 'MockTelemetryService' isn't properly capturing the event because of the way 'IEnvironmentService' is mocked in the setup.

You are likely hitting a dependency injection mismatch. Check your 'serviceCollection' instantiation in the test suite. You probably need to register the 'MockEnvironmentService' before the 'TelemetryService' is constructed.
That was it! I had the instantiation order flipped. Everything is passing now. I'm going to push these changes to a feature branch for internal testing before merging.
Excellent. Once you verify that the build environment doesn't trigger unexpected telemetry spikes, we can consider this secondary project fully integrated.
Wait, I noticed the telemetry logs are showing a 'Socket timeout' error in the 'TelemetryAppender' logic when trying to send these new events from certain regional nodes. Is the endpoint struggling?

That could be due to regional network restrictions. Check 'src/vs/platform/telemetry/common/telemetryAppender.ts'. We might need to add a fallback retry mechanism or a more robust timeout handler for outgoing requests.

I see it now. The 'maxRetries' is set to 3. I'll bump that to 5 and implement an exponential backoff. Hopefully, that should smooth out the connectivity issues without saturating the client's network.
Exponential backoff is definitely the right move. Make sure to use the standard 'setTimeout' approach and avoid blocking the main thread, as performance in the build pipeline is critical.
I’ve implemented the backoff in 'src/vs/platform/telemetry/common/telemetryAppender.ts'. I’m seeing much more stable behavior in my local reproduction script now.
Great work. It seems we've not only improved our license enforcement but also hardened our infrastructure against unreliable network conditions.
I'm ready to perform the final integration of this patch. I'll merge the feature branch into 'main' and keep an eye on the telemetry dashboard for the next few hours.
Keep an eye on the error logs as well. If you see any 'TelemetryTransmissionFailed' errors rising after the merge, don't hesitate to roll back the changes to the 'telemetryAppender'.
Will do. I'm tagging the PR as 'telemetry-resilience-update'. It’s nice to have this infrastructure ready in case we ever need to track similar issues again.
It’s a valuable addition. Being able to audit our codebase's distribution programmatically will save us a lot of headaches in the long run.
Deployment is complete. The telemetry pipeline is receiving data without errors, and the build scripts are still running in under 2 minutes. Success.
Fantastic result. You've handled this entire saga, from the initial issue triage to the technical hardening, with great professionalism. Now, let's get back to those sprint tasks.

Moving on, I need to address the technical debt in 'src/vs/workbench/services/extensions/common/extensionHostProcess.ts'. The way we handle lifecycle shutdown hooks is causing race conditions in some scenarios.
That module is sensitive. The 'ExtensionHostProcess' needs careful handling of the 'onDidTerminate' signal. What kind of race conditions are you observing during shutdown?
I'm seeing 'ExtensionHostTerminationError' when multiple extensions try to write to the local storage simultaneously as the process exits. I'm thinking of adding a flush queue.

A queue for flushing data is a solid pattern. Ensure you modify the 'ExtensionHostManager' to await these promises before final process exit in 'src/vs/workbench/services/extensions/node/extensionHostManager.ts'.
Good catch. I'll add an 'async flushStorage()' method that tracks pending write operations using a 'Promise.allSettled' approach to ensure we don't block on a single failed write.
Exactly, that prevents one hung extension from stalling the entire IDE shutdown. Remember to update the 'ExtensionHostProcessWorker' implementation as well.
I've drafted the changes. Running the unit tests now, but I suspect I might have broken the 'test-extension-lifecycle' suite in 'src/vs/workbench/test/browser/extensionHost.test.ts'.
Check your mocks in the test suite. If you changed the timing of 'terminate()', you might need to adjust the 'await' assertions to account for the new flush queue delay.
You were right. The test was failing because it asserted exit before the async flush completed. I added a small timeout in the test harness to allow the queue to drain.
Try to avoid 'setTimeout' in tests if possible. Can you use a 'deferred' promise or an event listener on the flush queue instead to keep tests deterministic?
I'll implement an 'onDidFlushComplete' event emitter in 'ExtensionHostManager'. That’s much cleaner than relying on arbitrary timing. Testing that now.
That is the standard VS Code way. It avoids flakiness and makes the extension host lifecycle much more predictable for our internal consumers.
Tests passed! The build is clean. I am refactoring 'src/vs/workbench/services/extensions/common/extensionHostMain.ts' to integrate this new shutdown sequence.
Excellent. Make sure to log a 'TelemetryWarning' if an extension takes too long to flush its state; we don't want the user's exit to hang forever.
Added a 5-second deadline for the flush process. If it exceeds that, we force terminate and report the offending extension ID via 'ITelemetryService'.
That covers the edge case nicely. Does the 'ExtensionHostProcess' report the specific plugin causing the delay in the telemetry payload?
Yes, I’m including the 'extensionId' in the metadata. This should help us identify which extensions are poorly behaving during shutdown.
This is a significant improvement. I'll review your PR once you push it to the 'ext-host-refactor' branch. Do you have documentation on the new API?
I’m writing the comments in 'src/vs/workbench/api/node/extHostExtensionService.ts' now. It should be clear for other contributors to follow the new lifecycle flow.
Perfect. Once documented, we'll be ready for a final code review and merge. Great work keeping the architecture stable while iterating on these fixes.
I've pushed the documentation updates to 'src/vs/workbench/api/node/extHostExtensionService.ts'. It clarifies the 'onDidFlushComplete' usage for third-party extensions.
The documentation looks thorough. I'll start the review process. How are you handling potential race conditions if an extension attempts to register a flush listener after termination has begun?
I added a state check in 'ExtensionHostManager'. If the shutdown phase is already 'Terminating', 'registerFlushListener' throws an error to prevent late registrations.
Good catch. That prevents unpredictable behavior. Are you using a specific error type, perhaps a 'LifecycleStateError', to help extension developers debug their timing?
Yes, I'm using a new 'LifecycleStateError' exported from 'src/vs/platform/lifecycle/common/lifecycle.ts'. It provides a clear message explaining why the registration failed.
That makes sense. It aligns with the existing architecture. Have you run the unit tests in 'src/vs/workbench/test/node/extensionHostManager.test.ts' to verify this behavior?
The tests passed. I also added a mock scenario where an extension hangs during flush, confirming the 5-second timeout triggers as expected.
Excellent. Testing for the timeout scenario is crucial. I’m running a full build on the 'ext-host-refactor' branch to ensure no regressions in other modules.
Build succeeded on my local machine. I am now double-checking the 'ITelemetryService' payloads in 'src/vs/platform/telemetry/common/telemetryUtils.ts' to confirm they are correctly formatted.
Looks good. The metadata structure is consistent with our logging standards. I'm satisfied with this implementation. Any final thoughts on the migration path?
We should probably send a memo to the extension team regarding this lifecycle change so they can prepare for the deprecation of the older shutdown handlers.
Agreed. I'll draft the internal communication once we merge the PR. It’s important to give them sufficient lead time for the transition.
Sounds like a plan. Should I also update the 'API' samples repository to demonstrate the usage of 'onDidFlushComplete'?
Yes, that would be very helpful. It provides a concrete reference for extension authors. Could you prepare a PR for the samples repo as well?
Will do. I'll link the PR for the samples in the main VS Code PR description so they are tracked together.
Perfect. Everything seems to be lined up. I’ll perform a final scan of the code changes in 'src/vs/workbench/services/extensions/common/extensionHostMain.ts' before approval.
Take your time. I'll be available if any questions arise during your final scan of the implementation.
The logic looks solid. No issues found. I’m ready to approve and merge this into the main branch once the final CI checks are done.
Great! I'll trigger the final CI run on the 'ext-host-refactor' branch now. Thanks for the help through this process.
My pleasure. This work really stabilizes the extension host shutdown process. I look forward to seeing this land in the next release.
The CI on 'ext-host-refactor' is failing with a timeout error in 'src/vs/workbench/test/browser/extensionHost.test.ts'. It seems like the teardown logic is hanging.

That is unexpected. Let's look at the logs. It seems 'onDidFlushComplete' is waiting for a signal from the internal 'ExtensionHostProcessWorker' that never arrives. Did we change the sequence of disposal?
I see it. I changed the order in 'src/vs/workbench/services/extensions/browser/extensionService.ts' to trigger the flush before the worker termination. Maybe the worker is blocking the event loop.
Ah, if the event loop is blocked, the promise won't resolve. Let's wrap the trigger in a 'setTimeout' to force a task switch, or better yet, verify the worker state before flushing.
Good call. I will modify 'src/vs/workbench/services/extensions/common/extensionHostMain.ts' to check the 'isTerminating' flag before initiating the flush procedure.
That sounds safer. While you are there, ensure the 'IDisposable' tracking in 'src/vs/base/common/lifecycle.ts' correctly handles the race condition where the host might be disposing simultaneously.
Updating the logic now. I'm adding an explicit 'abort' signal to the 'onDidFlushComplete' event emitter to ensure we don't hang indefinitely during test teardown.
Excellent. After you apply that, let's re-run the tests locally using 'gulp test --grep ExtensionHost'. If it passes, we should be clear.
The test passed! It seems the 'abort' signal successfully cleared the hanging promise in 'src/vs/workbench/test/browser/extensionHost.test.ts'.
That is a huge relief. The fix seems robust. Do you want to push this to the 'ext-host-refactor' branch and trigger the CI again?
Pushing now. I am also adding a small documentation comment in 'src/vs/workbench/services/extensions/common/extensions.ts' to explain why the order matters.
Documentation is key here. Given how complex the extension lifecycle is, future maintainers will appreciate that context. Are there any other potential side effects?
I've checked the telemetry reporting in 'src/vs/platform/telemetry/common/telemetryService.ts'. It seems unaffected by the changes, which is good news.
Glad to hear that. We definitely don't want to break our visibility into extension startup times. Everything seems to be in order for the merge.
I'll keep a close watch on the CI logs this time. If everything stays green, I'll squash the commits into a single clean PR.
Sounds perfect. Once it is squashed, please notify me, and I will finalize the approval in the GitHub UI for the main branch.
CI just finished successfully! All checks passed, including the integration tests. I'm squashing the changes now.
Great work. I see the PR update. I'll review the final squash one last time and then hit merge to 'main'.
Thanks for your guidance on the lifecycle management. It really helped navigate the edge cases in the extension host.
Anytime. It was a challenging but necessary refactor. Let's monitor the telemetry once this hits the next Insiders build.

I noticed the PR was merged, but I'm concerned about the impact on the VS Code web-based workbench. Should I re-examine 'src/vs/workbench/browser/web.main.ts' to ensure the extension service initialization holds up there?

That is a valid concern. The web version handles extensions slightly differently via the 'RemoteExtensionHostManager'. Check the 'src/vs/workbench/services/extensions/browser/webWorkerExtensionHost.ts' file as well to be safe.
Good call. Investigating 'webWorkerExtensionHost.ts' reveals that the constructor might initialize before our new hooks are fully registered. I might need a deferred promise here.

If the promise isn't awaited in the initialization sequence, we'll get race conditions. Consider adding a 'wait-for-registration' signal in 'src/vs/workbench/services/extensions/common/extensionHostProtocol.ts'.
Hypothesis: adding a 'registerReady' event emitter to the protocol will solve the race. I'm prototyping the changes now.
That should work. Ensure the emitter is correctly disposed of in the 'dispose()' method of 'ExtensionHostManager' to prevent memory leaks in the browser environment.
I've implemented the emitter. Running local tests with 'yarn test' against 'vs/workbench/test/browser/extensionService.test.ts'. Currently hitting a null pointer in the tests.
Check your 'initialize()' method in 'extensionService.ts'. If the protocol is disposed before the promise resolves, you'll see that null reference. Use an optional chaining operator.
That fixed the null pointer! Tests are passing now. However, I notice increased latency during the startup of the web extension host. Digging into the timing in 'telemetryService.ts'.
The extra latency is likely due to the blocking wait on the emitter. Perhaps we can make the registration lazy instead of blocking the entire main workbench thread?
Great idea. I'll refactor the 'registerReady' to use a non-blocking resolution strategy. Updating 'src/vs/workbench/services/extensions/common/extensions.ts' to use an async notification.
Perfect. If it remains async, the main thread will continue rendering while the extension host catches up. Test this against slow network conditions using the developer tools throttling.
Testing with 'Fast 3G' throttling in Chrome. The UI stays responsive now, and extensions load exactly when they are ready. The fix feels robust.
That sounds like a successful refinement. Have you verified that this doesn't negatively impact the desktop 'main.ts' entry point during the transition?
Verified. Desktop startup times are unchanged since the async path is only gated by the new protocol logic in the web-specific browser services.
Excellent. This keeps the desktop performant while solving the race condition in the web environment. Squash the new changes and I'll review.
Squashed the commits and pushed to the branch. The CI pipeline for the web tests is running now. I'm feeling confident about this final state.
I see the PR update. The logic in 'webWorkerExtensionHost.ts' is cleaner now. Merging this into 'main' and closing the associated tracking issue.
Thanks for all the help, this was a tricky piece of the extension host to refactor. I've learned a lot about the lifecycle hooks.
You are welcome. These platform-specific initialization issues are always the hardest. Glad we could resolve it properly before the release.

Since we resolved the extension host timing, should we look into the telemetry privacy concerns raised in issue #191229? Even though it's technically a policy issue, the user reports that unauthorized data might be leaking.

That's a sensitive topic. We should strictly limit our investigation to the code in 'src/vs/platform/telemetry/common/telemetryService.ts' to ensure no unexpected endpoints are being hit, regardless of the claims in that issue.

I'm checking 'telemetryService.ts' now. The 'AppInsights' integration looks standard, but I noticed a potential misconfiguration in the 'appender' initialization that might allow custom URI endpoints.
Good catch. Verify if the 'telemetryConfiguration' interface allows overriding the default collector URL. Check if 'getTelemetryEndpoint' is properly validating against our allowed domain list.
It doesn't seem to have strict validation. If I modify 'telemetryService.ts' to enforce a whitelist, we can prevent any third-party redirects.
Enforcing a hardcoded whitelist is a safe approach. Update the 'sendEvent' method to check the destination URI against a constant 'TELEMETRY_ALLOWED_DOMAINS' array.
I've drafted the change. I'm adding the whitelist to 'src/vs/platform/telemetry/common/telemetryUtils.ts' and referencing it in the 'telemetryService.ts' constructor.
Make sure you include a logging warning when a blocked domain is detected so we can monitor if this affects any legitimate internal plugins.
I've added the logger injection. Testing now with a unit test in 'test/unit/platform/telemetry/telemetryService.test.ts' that mocks an unauthorized endpoint.
The unit test in 'telemetryService.test.ts' should assert that the 'sendEvent' promise rejects or logs an error. Are you seeing the expected output?
Yes, it correctly identifies the blocked endpoint. The telemetry service now drops the transmission instead of attempting a connection. The fix is clean.
This effectively silences any unauthorized data exfiltration attempts. It seems like a solid, proactive security patch for our current architecture.
Wait, I should also check if 'src/vs/workbench/services/configuration/common/configuration.ts' allows users to bypass this via workspace settings. I don't want them overriding the whitelist.
Good thinking. Audit the configuration service to see if 'telemetry.url' is marked as a restricted setting that cannot be overridden in 'settings.json'.
It is not currently marked restricted. I'll update 'configurationRegistry.ts' to make it 'application' scope only.
That prevents workspace-level tampering. Once you push that change, let's verify that the 'ConfigurationService' rejects the attempt at startup.
Verified. Trying to change the URL in a local folder's '.vscode/settings.json' now results in an 'Invalid setting' diagnostic error.
Excellent. That locks down the entire telemetry pipeline. The logic seems very robust now.
Everything is ready for a final PR. I've updated the documentation in the code to reflect the new security constraints.
Perfect. Submit the PR, and I'll perform a final scan of the commits. You've handled a complex security improvement effectively.
I have pushed the changes to the 'telemetry-security-patch' branch. I see that the CI pipeline is triggering. Are there any edge cases regarding the 'IConfigurationService' I might have missed?
The CI looks green. Regarding 'IConfigurationService', consider the 'onDidChangeConfiguration' event. If an application-scoped setting is updated, does the telemetry service re-initialize properly?
It should. I added a listener in 'src/vs/platform/telemetry/common/telemetryService.ts' that re-validates the URL against the whitelist whenever the application configuration changes.
Smart. By hooking into the event, you ensure that even if the app state changes, the restricted scope remains enforced. Have you tested this with a dynamic reload?
Yes, I simulated a config update via the debug console. The service immediately detected the restriction and dropped the active connection. No memory leaks detected.
Excellent. Memory safety is key here. Since we are modifying 'src/vs/platform/configuration/common/configurationRegistry.ts', did you update the schema documentation?
Yes, I added a deprecation notice and a 'restricted' flag to the JSON schema. This should make it clear to extensions that this setting is off-limits.
Perfect. The schema updates in 'configurationRegistry.ts' are essential for the 'Settings Editor' UI to show the correct lock icon.
The 'Settings Editor' now correctly displays a lock next to the field. It seems the UI layer consumes the schema changes automatically without needing extra code.
That is how the framework is designed to work. It saves us from writing custom UI logic. Are you ready to merge the PR into 'main'?
I am. I've rebased against the latest 'main' branch and addressed a small conflict in 'src/vs/workbench/contrib/preferences/browser/preferencesRenderers.ts'.
The merge conflict in 'preferencesRenderers.ts' is expected given how active that file is. Did you ensure your registry change didn't conflict with existing telemetry providers?
The telemetry providers use their own internal configs, so my changes to 'configurationRegistry.ts' should not impact their operational parameters.
Sounds good. Make sure to run the unit tests one last time in 'src/vs/platform/telemetry/test/common/telemetryService.test.ts'.
Running the tests now. All 45 tests in 'telemetryService.test.ts' passed, including the new security test case for the restricted URL.
That gives me confidence in the stability of the change. Submit the squash-and-merge request now.
Done. The PR is merged. Now I'm checking the logs to see if the telemetry endpoint correctly rejects invalid hostnames.
The integration tests in the staging environment should confirm this shortly. Keep an eye on the telemetry backend error metrics.
The metrics are showing a spike in 'AccessDenied' errors, which confirms the block is working exactly as intended.
That is exactly what we wanted to see. Mission accomplished, the telemetry pipeline is now fully locked down.

I noticed in the telemetry logs that some VS Code extensions are still trying to connect to unauthorized endpoints. Is there a way to notify the extension host to handle these rejections more gracefully?

You should look into 'src/vs/workbench/api/common/extHostTelemetry.ts'. We can implement a mechanism to propagate an error event back to the extension host if a request is blocked by the telemetry service.
Right, I see the 'TelemetryService' class. I could potentially wrap the 'publicLog' method to check for a rejection status and throw an 'ExtensionTelemetryError' which the host could catch.
That sounds like a solid plan. Keep in mind that we need to avoid leaking information about the blacklist to the extension itself for security reasons.
Agreed. I will modify 'src/vs/platform/telemetry/common/telemetryService.ts' to return a generic status code instead of a specific reason why the endpoint was blocked.
Good approach. While you are there, double-check 'src/vs/platform/telemetry/common/telemetryUtils.ts' to ensure that common configuration helpers aren't leaking those details either.
Good catch. 'telemetryUtils.ts' does contain some logging helpers that might need updating to scrub the outgoing metadata before serialization.
Exactly. Let's start with a refactor of 'telemetryService.ts' and then run the unit tests in 'telemetryService.test.ts' again to verify no regressions.
I've drafted the changes. The 'publicLog' method now returns a 'TelemetryResult' enum, which seems much cleaner for the extension host to handle.
The enum approach is definitely better than relying on boolean returns. How does this look for the integration tests in 'telemetryService.test.ts'?
I added a mock 'ExtHostTelemetry' test case. It correctly reports an 'AccessDenied' result back to the host without exposing the internal URL configuration.
Perfect. Does the extension host gracefully handle that error, or does it crash the extension's telemetry logger?
It seems the host logs a warning and continues. I've verified this by checking the output channel in 'src/vs/workbench/contrib/output/common/outputChannel.ts'.
That's exactly what we want. Can you ensure the error is silenced if the developer has debugging turned off in their 'settings.json'?
I will add a conditional check using the 'IConfigurationService' in 'telemetryService.ts' to respect the 'telemetry.debug' setting.
Sounds reasonable. Let's make sure that change doesn't introduce any extra latency to the logging process.
